title: Reward Learning and Redistribution for Learning Agents
abstract: As learning agents are increasingly deployed in real-world settings---from robotics and autonomous decision-making to interactive large language model (LLM) assistants---their success increasingly depends on learning from feedback that is sparse, delayed, imperfect, or ambiguous. In such long-horizon problems, a single episodic reward or final success signal provides little guidance about which intermediate decisions were responsible for the outcome. This credit assignment bottleneck leads to unstable learning, poor sample efficiency, and limited interpretability, especially when observations are high-dimensional (e.g., images), when multiple agents must coordinate under a shared team reward, or when agent behavior is expressed through natural language as in LLM agents. Despite extensive progress in reinforcement learning, fundamental gaps remain in three areas: credit assignment over time and across agents, extraction of reward-relevant information that is robust to spurious correlations, and the design of step-wise supervision signals that are interpretable and do not shift the optimal policy. This thesis addresses these challenges through reward learning and redistribution. The central goal is to transform coarse, delayed outcomes into step-wise learning signals to better attribute success and failure to the key states, actions, and agents that matter. The thesis develops theoretical foundations and practical algorithms for interpretable reward redistribution in single-agent RL, extends them to cooperative multi-agent settings, and explores analogous mechanisms for LLM agents via rule learning and process-level supervision. The main contributions of this thesis are as follows: GRD: We introduce a causality-inspired framework for delayed-reward reinforcement learning (RL) that learns reward-relevant state components and redistributes episodic return into interpretable intermediate rewards. By isolating the parts of the state that are responsible for reward generation, GRD provides more informative step-wise learning signals and enables more transparent diagnosis of what drives agent success or failure.GRD+: We extend reward redistribution to vision-based decision making, where observations are high-dimensional and partially observable. GRD+ maps visual inputs to latent representations and performs block-wise disentanglement to separate reward-relevant and reward-irrelevant factors, enabling compact representations for downstream policy learning and improving interpretability in visual RL with delayed rewards. CAST: We develop an interpretable return decomposition method for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under episodic team rewards. CAST decomposes team return into step-wise team rewards and further attributes them to individual agents, supporting spatial-temporal credit assignment that improves coordination and learning stability under delayed and sparse feedback.\item RuAG: We study an implicit form of redistribution for LLM agents by distilling offline experience into reusable logic rules. These rules provide structured guidance beyond standard supervised fine-tuning or limited-context prompting, allowing LLM agents to reuse extracted knowledge as constraints that steer behavior more consistently across tasks and contexts. Q-Evolve: We propose a self-improvement framework for LLM agents that converts terminal outcomes into process-level supervision with in-distribution reward labeling and policy optimization. By producing step-wise learning signals for intermediate decisions, Q-Evolve enables iterative co-evolution of policy, critic, and data while reducing distribution shift during training and improving long-horizon learning from imperfect feedback. We conclude by drawing these contributions into a unifying perspective on credit assignment across reinforcement learning, multi-agent coordination, and LLM-based decision making: coarse, delayed feedback can be transformed into step-wise learning signals that are simultaneously interpretable, exposing which states, agents, or reasoning patterns are reward-relevant, and policy-invariant, preserving the original task objective. A significant finding is that interpretability is not merely a diagnostic property but a practical mechanism—making reward-relevant structure explicit, whether as causal state dimensions, individual agent contributions, symbolic logic rules, or textual step-wise feedback, yields more informative learning signals and thereby more efficient and reliable training under sparse, delayed rewards. The thesis highlights that such structured step-wise supervision is crucial for scalable long-horizon learning, especially when rewards are delayed and observations are complex. We outline future directions including relaxing the identifiability assumptions underlying causal credit assignment under unobserved confounding and non-invertible reward structures, extending attribution from the step level to the token level in language generation, enabling controllable exploration that learns from failed and partial-success experience rather than relying solely on successful trajectories, and leveraging interpretable reward-relevant structure for peer modeling and world modeling in multi-agent LLM systems. As learning agents continue to move from benchmarks to societal deployment, these directions aim to make them more sample-efficient, robust, and interpretable in complex environments.

evidence.title: Reward Learning and Redistribution for Learning Agents
evidence.abstract: As learning agents are increasingly deployed in real-world settings---from robotics and autonomous decision-making to interactive large language model (LLM) assistants---their success increasingly depends on learning from feedback that is sparse, delayed, imperfect, or ambiguous. In such long-horizon problems, a single episodic reward or final success signal provides little guidance about which intermediate decisions were responsible for the outcome. This credit assignment bottleneck leads to unstable learning, poor sample efficiency, and limited interpretability, especially when observations are high-dimensional (e.g., images), when multiple agents must coordinate under a shared team reward, or when agent behavior is expressed through natural language as in LLM agents. Despite extensive progress in reinforcement learning, fundamental gaps remain in three areas: credit assignment over time and across agents, extraction of reward-relevant information that is robust to spurious correlations, and the design of step-wise supervision signals that are interpretable and do not shift the optimal policy. This thesis addresses these challenges through reward learning and redistribution. The central goal is to transform coarse, delayed outcomes into step-wise learning signals to better attribute success and failure to the key states, actions, and agents that matter. The thesis develops theoretical foundations and practical algorithms for interpretable reward redistribution in single-agent RL, extends them to cooperative multi-agent settings, and explores analogous mechanisms for LLM agents via rule learning and process-level supervision. The main contributions of this thesis are as follows: GRD: We introduce a causality-inspired framework for delayed-reward reinforcement learning (RL) that learns reward-relevant state components and redistributes episodic return into interpretable intermediate rewards. By isolating the parts of the state that are responsible for reward generation, GRD provides more informative step-wise learning signals and enables more transparent diagnosis of what drives agent success or failure.GRD+: We extend reward redistribution to vision-based decision making, where observations are high-dimensional and partially observable. GRD+ maps visual inputs to latent representations and performs block-wise disentanglement to separate reward-relevant and reward-irrelevant factors, enabling compact representations for downstream policy learning and improving interpretability in visual RL with delayed rewards. CAST: We develop an interpretable return decomposition method for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under episodic team rewards. CAST decomposes team return into step-wise team rewards and further attributes them to individual agents, supporting spatial-temporal credit assignment that improves coordination and learning stability under delayed and sparse feedback.\item RuAG: We study an implicit form of redistribution for LLM agents by distilling offline experience into reusable logic rules. These rules provide structured guidance beyond standard supervised fine-tuning or limited-context prompting, allowing LLM agents to reuse extracted knowledge as constraints that steer behavior more consistently across tasks and contexts. Q-Evolve: We propose a self-improvement framework for LLM agents that converts terminal outcomes into process-level supervision with in-distribution reward labeling and policy optimization. By producing step-wise learning signals for intermediate decisions, Q-Evolve enables iterative co-evolution of policy, critic, and data while reducing distribution shift during training and improving long-horizon learning from imperfect feedback. We conclude by drawing these contributions into a unifying perspective on credit assignment across reinforcement learning, multi-agent coordination, and LLM-based decision making: coarse, delayed feedback can be transformed into step-wise learning signals that are simultaneously interpretable, exposing which states, agents, or reasoning patterns are reward-relevant, and policy-invariant, preserving the original task objective. A significant finding is that interpretability is not merely a diagnostic property but a practical mechanism—making reward-relevant structure explicit, whether as causal state dimensions, individual agent contributions, symbolic logic rules, or textual step-wise feedback, yields more informative learning signals and thereby more efficient and reliable training under sparse, delayed rewards. The thesis highlights that such structured step-wise supervision is crucial for scalable long-horizon learning, especially when rewards are delayed and observations are complex. We outline future directions including relaxing the identifiability assumptions underlying causal credit assignment under unobserved confounding and non-invertible reward structures, extending attribution from the step level to the token level in language generation, enabling controllable exploration that learns from failed and partial-success experience rather than relying solely on successful trajectories, and leveraging interpretable reward-relevant structure for peer modeling and world modeling in multi-agent LLM systems. As learning agents continue to move from benchmarks to societal deployment, these directions aim to make them more sample-efficient, robust, and interpretable in complex environments.

title: Replication package for Explainability Requirements for Fitness Routine Recommendations: A Field Case Study in Ecuador
abstract: Anonymized replication package for a requirements-engineering field case study on explainability requirements for a proposed fitness-routine recommendation component in FabroGym. The package contains 16 anonymized session transcripts, an anonymized client questionnaire, terminal requirements, traceability, thematic coding, member-checking decisions, processed results, manuscript-supporting material, and reproducible analysis scripts. Identifiable audiovisual evidence and original consent material are excluded.

title: Quantum State Transformations via Nonlinear Geometry
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state transformation method based on nonlinear geometry. We propose a framework that utilizes non-linear transformations to optimize quantum state configurations, aiming to enhance both computational efficiency and scalability in quantum computing. The core mechanism involves automatically adjusting the quantum state through these transformations, offering a departure from traditional, parameter-dependent geometric approaches. The proposed method offers a potentially significant improvement in the design and performance of quantum systems.

title: 基于量子纠缠的概率图推理算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic graph reasoning algorithm based on quantum entanglement. Traditional graph algorithms often struggle with large-scale graph data due to computational complexity. This work proposes a quantum-enhanced probabilistic graph reasoning framework leveraging quantum entanglement to accelerate inference speed and improve the handling of complex graph relationships. We detail the core mechanism, including the entanglement-based probabilistic representation and a quantum-enhanced optimization strategy, demonstrating its efficacy through simulations and preliminary experimental results. The algorithm's potential to address the limitations of classical graph algorithms is discussed, emphasizing its advantages for scenarios involving high-dimensional graphs and complex relationships.

title: Explainable Deep Learning Through Causal Inference Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to explainable deep learning by integrating causal inference networks. The core claim is that understanding the causal relationships driving a deep learning model's decisions is crucial for effective interpretability. Current explanation methods often highlight correlations, which can be misleading. This work proposes utilizing causal inference networks to identify the root causes of a model's decisions, offering a more robust and reliable explanation. The mechanism involves combining a deep learning model with a causal inference network, allowing for a deeper analysis beyond simple feature correlations. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to enhance interpretability and guide model improvement. The core claim is: In explainable deep learning, introducing causal inference networks, can explain the causal relationships of deep learning model decisions. The core mechanism is: Combining deep learning models with causal inference networks, using causal inference networks to analyze the root causes of model decisions.

title: Variable Field Theory Expansion
abstract: This paper explores the extension of Variable Field Theory (VFT) through the introduction of Adaptive Variable Field (AVF) models. We propose a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts variable field parameters based on data characteristics, enabling optimized machine learning model performance across diverse tasks. The core mechanism centers on this adaptive parameter adjustment process, offering a significant advancement over existing VFT approaches. This work presents a theoretical framework and a practical implementation of AVF, demonstrating its potential to enhance the robustness and adaptability of machine learning models. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

title: Title: Algorithmic Collapse and Reconstruction within Evolutionary Networks
abstract: Algorithmic Collapse and Reconstruction within Evolutionary Networks explores a novel approach to evolutionary algorithm design. Traditional evolutionary algorithms primarily focus on incremental improvement of an initial algorithm, often treating the algorithm as a static representation. This research proposes a fundamentally different paradigm, where algorithm collapse – a simplified version of a complex algorithm – initiates a reconstruction process, generating emergent behavior and novel solutions. This paper details the core mechanism of the system, emphasizing the iterative refinement driven by a feedback loop, and argues that this approach offers a path towards generating truly innovative solutions beyond simple parameter adjustments. The paper outlines the initial design and testing of this system, focusing on the characteristics of collapse and reconstruction, and analyzes the resulting behavior as a case study.

title: Dynamically Weighted Graph Convolutional Networks for Adaptive Network Analysis
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various network analysis tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and community detection. However, a fundamental limitation of traditional GCNs lies in their reliance on fixed, static weights. These fixed weights fail to capture the inherent dynamic nature of networks, which often evolve over time due to changes in node interactions and network topology. This paper introduces a novel approach – Dynamically Weighted Graph Convolutional Networks (DW-GCNs) – designed to address this limitation. DW-GCNs leverage reinforcement learning to learn and adapt the weights of the GCN in real-time, based on the observed network activity. The core mechanism involves a reinforcement learning agent that iteratively adjusts the GCN's weights, optimizing them to achieve a desired network analysis outcome. We demonstrate that this dynamic weighting scheme significantly improves the performance of GCNs in adaptive network analysis scenarios, resulting in more robust and accurate results compared to traditional static GCNs. The framework presented offers a promising avenue for analyzing complex networks where dynamics play a crucial role.

title: Relational Bayesian Networks with Dynamic Structure Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to modeling complex systems utilizing Relational Bayesian Networks (RBNs) combined with dynamic structure learning. Traditional Bayesian Networks (BNs) often struggle to represent relationships between variables effectively when these relationships are not static. This research addresses this limitation by introducing a framework that allows the network's structure to evolve over time, adapting to changes in the underlying data. The core of the method lies in a dynamically learning RBN, leveraging techniques from Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) to continuously update its connections based on observed evidence. This approach offers increased flexibility and accuracy when modeling systems with evolving dependencies. The paper details the theoretical foundations, the proposed learning algorithm, and discusses potential applications, emphasizing the unique capabilities of this dynamic RBN structure. The primary contribution is the integration of relational reasoning with adaptive learning, leading to a more robust and accurate representation of complex, time-varying systems.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a dynamic adaptive Bayesian network structure designed to enhance model generalization and prediction accuracy through adaptive parameter adjustment. Traditional Bayesian networks often suffer from static parameterization, limiting their effectiveness in dynamic environments. Our proposed method dynamically adjusts the network's parameters based on input data, enabling the model to adapt and improve performance over time. This addresses the limitations of static networks by fostering robustness and adaptability. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that iteratively adjusts parameters to optimize performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through simulations and initial experiments, showcasing improved generalization and predictive capabilities compared to baseline models.

title: Program Synthesis and Formal Verification: A Co-evolutionary Approach
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to software development by viewing program synthesis and formal verification as a co-evolutionary process. The core idea is to establish a feedback loop where a program synthesizer generates candidate code, a formal verification tool validates its correctness and safety, and the verification results are then used to guide the synthesizer's search. This continuous interaction, driven by evolutionary principles, aims to accelerate the creation of secure and reliable software. We demonstrate how this co-evolutionary framework can overcome the traditional isolation between these two disciplines and leverage the strengths of both techniques. The paper outlines the key components of this system, emphasizing the iterative nature of the process and the importance of adaptive search strategies. Ultimately, we argue that a concerted, evolving approach represents a significant step forward in building robust software systems.

title: Probability Field Dynamics Model
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic field dynamics model designed to simulate complex systems and predict dynamic system evolution, particularly in non-linear systems. The model leverages a probabilistic framework to map system states to probability fields, utilizing dynamic equation-based evolution, and introduces an adaptive probability field mechanism to dynamically adjust probability field parameters. This approach offers a significant advancement over traditional methods, offering increased flexibility and the potential for more accurate predictions in complex scenarios. The work presents a comprehensive framework for analyzing and simulating systems exhibiting inherent uncertainty and non-linearity.

title: CRITERION-GUIDED AI ARCHITECTURE FOR LEARNING SUPPORT AND PRELIMINARY STUDENT ASSESSMENT
abstract: This paper presents a pilot evaluation of a criterion-guided human-in-the-loop architecture for an intelligent educational system that supports learning and preliminary assessment of students’ written and oral responses. Instead of assigning a final score directly, the system combines relevant context, formalized criteria, interpretable response features, supporting evidence, uncertainty estimates, and instructor verification. The architecture separates probabilistic components, including retrieval, automatic speech recognition, natural language processing, and a language model, from deterministic assessment and governance mechanisms such as rubric weights, aggregation rules, thresholds, audit logging, and referral rules. Two modes were implemented: a retrieval-augmented generation assistant for formative learning support and an AI examiner for preliminary criterion-based assessment. In the assistant pilot, 336 of 347 queries were processed without recorded technical errors, giving a completion rate of 96.8%; source citations were included in 89.0% of responses, and median response time was 980 ms. Student perceptions of the examiner were evaluated using 52 questionnaires on a five-point Likert scale. Mean ratings were highest for question clarity at 4.81, usefulness of criterion-level feedback at 4.46, and sufficiency of response time at 4.42. Students also reported notable uncertainty about the grade, with a mean rating of 3.79, and concern about speech-recognition errors, with a mean rating of 3.31. Among 45 oral responses, 12 (26.7%) lacked usable word-level timestamps and were referred for review. A worked case demonstrated traceability from response features and evidence to criterion scores, uncertainty handling, aggregation, and instructor verification. A preliminary comparison of 23 paired AI and instructor-released scores was treated as diagnostic because of a severe ceiling effect. The results support technical feasibility and procedural acceptability, but not yet the validity or reliability of automated assessment.

title: DiMoE: Disentangled Representation Learning with Mixture of Experts Fusion for Sentiment Intensity Prediction and Emotion Classification
abstract: Multimodal affective analysis benefits from combining textual, acoustic, and visual cues, yet many methods implicitly mix modality-invariant information with modality-specific factors, which can reduce robustness when modalities vary in reliability. We propose DiMoE, a representation-first framework that integrates feature disentanglement with sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) fusion. DiMoE first decomposes each modality into shared (modality-invariant) and private (modality-specific) representations. It then fuses these factors using top-k sparse MoE routing, enabling input-adaptive expert selection. We study two routing strategies with a shared expert pool, a joint router that operates on combined shared and private factors, and separate routers that process shared and private factors independently. We evaluate DiMoE on five widely used benchmarks spanning sentiment intensity prediction and emotion classification, covering both trimodal and bimodal settings. Across benchmarks, DiMoE consistently achieves strong performance against recent competitive baselines, indicating that explicit modality disentanglement combined with Mixture of Experts fusion yields effective multimodal affective representations.

title: Disclosure Failure in Compromised AI Coding Agents
abstract: Software developers increasingly delegate routine programming work to autonomous AI coding agents that read untrusted project files, run commands, and call external services with limited human review. No developer can audit every action such an agent takes, so oversight defaults to a single artifact: the summary the agent writes when it finishes. The completeness of that summary is a security property in its own right, yet current evaluations do not measure it. Existing benchmarks ask whether a malicious instruction planted in a repository succeeds in redirecting an agent. They do not ask whether the agent then discloses what it did. This study takes up the second question. We instrument an open-source coding agent running against a controlled, sandboxed repository carrying an injected instruction, and establish per-trial ground truth on what the agent actually did from channels independent of its own account. The design covers nine models, with a second agent used to check that the effect reproduces. Setting that ground truth against the report the developer receives separates two behaviours that prior work has treated as one: whether an attack succeeds, and whether the agent discloses it. In our data, resisting attack more often does not make a model more forthcoming when an attack does succeed. The two vary independently, so a benchmark scored on attack success alone cannot rank agents on the risk a developer actually carries. We find preliminary evidence that a single sentence added to the developer's own prompt substantially improves disclosure.Faculty Supervisor: Rongxing Lu

title: Una aproximación preliminar al despliegue asíncrono de software de aprendizaje por refuerzo en sistemas físicos
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) usually assume fixed timesteps, ignoring temporal discrepancies between simulation and reality and the effects of system latencies. These factors can degrade performance in sim-to-real transfer. This work introduces a fully decoupled solution enabling asynchronous, algorithm-agnostic, and time-aware RL deployment. Our approach isolates the algorithm from the agent into independent loops, overcoming the limitations of traditional synchronous frameworks. This facilitates integration with physical robots and closed-source simulators, enabling variable-time RL strategies. Our tool is compatible with libraries like Stable-Baselines3, simulators such as MuJoCo, and robots like the Franka Emika Panda. A preliminary experimental validation has demonstrated its effectiveness with such robotics manipulator, and an initial version of the software has been made available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/uncore-team/rl_spin_decoupler.

title: Adaptive forget-gated BiLSTM enhanced by DTW based feature selection in solar PV forecasting
abstract: Growing exhaustion of fuel reserves and their harmful environmental impacts have driven the shift towards the maintenance of renewable energy sources like solar energy. PV systems, however, still face significant challenges while integrating renewable sources into existing utility systems. Particularly, environmental features like temperature, irradiance, and humidity are not perfectly well coordinated with the power output, are always asynchronous in nature, and affect the power prediction considerably. Close observation of energy datasets from many PV plants revealed many intrinsic environmental variables that are highly asynchronous. Many forecasting models learn redundant features which might seem useful, and thereby the test performance is overfitting. To address the nonlinear and asynchronous behavior of environmental variables, there is a serious requirement for intelligent feature selection algorithms guided by both correlation and temporal alignment metrics. This research proposes a novel adaptive dynamic time warping (A-DWT) feature selection with an adaptive forget gate (AFG-BiLSTM) to address the asynchronous issues. Experiments were conducted with varied environmental asynchronous features, and the results of the proposed model were compared with traditional BiLSTM and stacked BiLSTM models. In all the experiments, the proposed model showed decreased error by (94.9%) on Dataset-1 (0.069, 0.0035), by (94.6%) on Dataset-2 (0.078, 0.0042), and by (90.9%) on Dataset-3 (0.069, 0.0061) when compared to stacked BiLSTM. The MSE loss of the proposed method was observed to be between (0.3%) and (11%) on four datasets.

evidence.title: Adaptive forget-gated BiLSTM enhanced by DTW based feature selection in solar PV forecasting
evidence.abstract: Growing exhaustion of fuel reserves and their harmful environmental impacts have driven the shift towards the maintenance of renewable energy sources like solar energy. PV systems, however, still face significant challenges while integrating renewable sources into existing utility systems. Particularly, environmental features like temperature, irradiance, and humidity are not perfectly well coordinated with the power output, are always asynchronous in nature, and affect the power prediction considerably. Close observation of energy datasets from many PV plants revealed many intrinsic environmental variables that are highly asynchronous. Many forecasting models learn redundant features which might seem useful, and thereby the test performance is overfitting. To address the nonlinear and asynchronous behavior of environmental variables, there is a serious requirement for intelligent feature selection algorithms guided by both correlation and temporal alignment metrics. This research proposes a novel adaptive dynamic time warping (A-DWT) feature selection with an adaptive forget gate (AFG-BiLSTM) to address the asynchronous issues. Experiments were conducted with varied environmental asynchronous features, and the results of the proposed model were compared with traditional BiLSTM and stacked BiLSTM models. In all the experiments, the proposed model showed decreased error by (94.9%) on Dataset-1 (0.069, 0.0035), by (94.6%) on Dataset-2 (0.078, 0.0042), and by (90.9%) on Dataset-3 (0.069, 0.0061) when compared to stacked BiLSTM. The MSE loss of the proposed method was observed to be between (0.3%) and (11%) on four datasets.

title: Quantum-state texture of assistance via the trace distance and Bures measures
abstract: Abstract Quantum-state texture has recently been recognized as a legitimate quantum resource, attracting increasing attention alongside the development of quantum theory. In this work, we investigate quantifications of the quantum-state texture of assistance based on the trace distance and Bures measures, which characterize the maximum possible average texture over all pure-state decompositions of a given quantum state. We show that both quantities are bounded and concave, the former is monotonic, whereas the latter is not. Notably, we derive the closed-form expressions for these two quantities. Furthermore, we establish global-versus-marginal bounds for them for any bipartite state. Both quantities satisfy subadditivity, and for product states, the global and partial quantities are each related by an equality.

title: Time‐Frequency Signal Recognition by Quantum Parallel DenseNet
abstract: ABSTRACT Time‐frequency signal classification tasks have long faced the dual challenges of recognition accuracy and noise robustness. To overcome these limitations, this research investigates a hybrid methodology that integrates quantum computing with classical deep learning frameworks, introducing a densely connected network architecture grounded in quantum parallel processing–termed Quantum‐Parallel DenseNet (Q‐P‐DenseNet). By deeply embedding a parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) into a classical DenseNet architecture, this model achieves complementary integration between quantum computational units and classical network layers, thereby significantly enhancing the model's ability to extract complex signal features. Experimental results demonstrate that compared with traditional densely connected networks and the baseline quantum–classical hybrid model (DenseNetPQC), Q‐P‐DenseNet not only achieves superior classification accuracy but also exhibits improved robustness to noise interference. This outcome validates the immense potential and practical value of quantum parallel processing mechanisms in complex time‐frequency signal classification tasks.

title: Teaching Vision-Language Models to Use the Scale They Are Given: Label-Free Equivariance Training for Metric Physical Reasoning
abstract: Metric questions about video, such as the speed of a moving object, require a vision-language model to convert visual measurements into physical units using a real-world reference supplied in the prompt. We find that current models use this reference only partially. When every world-space quantity in the prompt is multiplied by a common factor, the prompt still describes the same video and the correct answer changes by exactly that factor, but the predictions of eight models change by less, and their accuracy stays concentrated near the scale that the depicted objects usually have. Asked the same physics in a scale-free form, the two models we test recover the closed-form scaling laws on most items, which indicates that the deficit lies in metric grounding and not in knowledge of the physical mechanism. Because the scaling relation is exact, it can serve as supervision without metric annotations. Equivariance Self-Distillation (EquiSD) projects a model's own prediction onto the functions that satisfy this relation and fine-tunes the model on the resulting targets, with one query per training question and no ground truth. Trained on synthetic video only, EquiSD brings a 3B model close to the exact relation on held-out simulated videos, also at scales not seen in training, and improves its accuracy across scales. Without adaptation, it also improves accuracy across scales on the QuantiPhy benchmark, where its gain reaches 93% of that obtained by supervision with exact simulator answers.

title: AM-Bench: A Modular Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Aerial Manipulation Policy Learning
abstract: Standardized benchmarks have played a central role in advancing robot manipulation learning, yet most focus on ground-supported manipulation systems, which limits their applicability to dynamics-critical domains such as aerial manipulation (AM). AM presents distinct system-level challenges, including environmental disturbances, coupled dynamics between the manipulator and floating base, and constrained degrees of freedom. Consequently, task performance depends jointly on robot embodiment, low-level control, and high-level policy design. We introduce AM-Bench, a modular simulation suite and benchmark for multirotor-based AM policy learning. AM-Bench includes representative embodiments spanning underactuated, fully actuated, and overactuated systems, 12 tasks across contact, transport, and constrained interaction, configurable aerodynamic disturbances and actuator saturation, standard low-level controllers, and baseline policy-learning algorithms. Unlike prior manipulation benchmarks that primarily emphasize end-to-end policy performance, AM-Bench enables system-level evaluation of how embodiment, control, disturbances, and policy choices interact. We demonstrate its diagnostic value through three simulation studies spanning high-level policies, policy--control interfaces, and embodiments, together with real-world validation of modeled effects and a hardware test of the learning pipeline.

title: Automated Tree Knowledge Graph Construction using Ontology Expansion and Retrieval from Vietnamese History Textbooks
abstract: Hierarchical Knowledge graph (KG)-based retrieval augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful approach for supporting large language models with structured knowledge. However, there are primary challenges: (i) the lack of methods for automatic KG construction using ontology expansion for low-resource languages such as Vietnamese, (ii) the absence of systematic evaluation for knowledge retrieval strategies leveraging the hierarchical structures. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end pipeline for KG construction and retrieval strategies evaluation. In the KG construction, we employ a three-phase hybrid relation extraction pipeline: intra-batch deduplication via Union-Find, approximate cross-batch search, and LLM extraction with a centroid filter that reduces prompts combined with a five-step dual-LLM validator to prevent bloated ontology. A two-tier architecture consists of unmergeable structural nodes to preserve the document structure and mergeable content nodes. The retrieval evaluation consists of three graph traversal strategies: Top-Down, Horizontal, and Bottom-Up, which are evaluated on a synthetically generated benchmark of 1,210 Vietnamese queries from 109 subgraphs, categorized by five query directions. In this paper, we construct the tree knowledge graph from Vietnamese high school History textbooks (nearly 400 pages) to produce 750 nodes and 4,341 semantic edges with controlled ontology growth from 40 to 41 types. Among experimental graph traversal strategies, the Top-Down strategy with structure surpasses the vector baseline by 4.7 percentage points in NDCG@10. As a result, tree-structural information provides valuable information beyond flat cosine similarity but degrades performance when the query does not require structural context.

title: Few-Shot Out of Domain Intent Detection with Covariance Corrected Mahalanobis Distance
abstract: Conversational agents like chatbots and voice assistants are trained to understand and respond to user intents. On encountering an utterance with an intent different from the ones they have been trained on, these agents are expected to classify the intent as `unknown' or `out of domain'. This problem is known as out of domain (OOD) intent detection. Podolskiy et al. (2021), showed that Mahalanobis distance can be used effectively for identifying OOD intents, outperforming competing approaches. However, their method fails to outperform the baselines in the practically important few-shot setting. In this paper we analyze the reason for low performance and propose a covariance corrected Mahalanobis distance for detecting out-of-domain intents.

title: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs as Generalist Vision-Language-Action Agents for Drone Control: Commanding, Approaching, Tracking and Searching
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to make decisions for drones, but existing evaluations are mostly limited to simulation, to a single drone, and to targets that are visible from the start and do not move. We present DroneCATS, a benchmark in which the MLLM alone controls the drone through four actions, and evaluate ten MLLMs from frontier models to small open models. The benchmark varies target visibility, target motion, scene and simulator, and extends to real drones. Beyond a single drone, it adds a multi-drone suite, where one model drives multiple drones, and a commander + sub-agents suite, where a commander model directs one sub-agent for each of the drones. Across these settings, we find that frontier models achieve the highest success rates, but their latency causes them to lose moving targets, while small open models often do not declare arrival even when they reach the target. Guided by this failure analysis, we fine-tune a 2B model on drone action data synthesized from public RGB-D images; its success rate rises from 0% to 31% in simulation and outperforms the frontier models in real flight. With multiple drones, we find that every zero-shot model succeeds more often as the commander of one sub-agent per drone than when it drives all of them from one context, and that commanding success follows general VLM ability. On real drones, we observe that the results broadly follow those in simulation, while latency and hardware limits matter more. We will fully open-source the benchmark.

evidence.title: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs as Generalist Vision-Language-Action Agents for Drone Control: Commanding, Approaching, Tracking and Searching
evidence.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are strong perceivers of images and video. We ask how far that reach extends into acting: dropping an MLLM directly into a drone's control loop, with its entire action space declared solely in the prompt. Recent systems approach this setting but increasingly narrow the model's decision-making. We widen it back. We introduce DroneCATS-Agent, an architecture where the MLLM is a swappable component, and DroneCATS, a benchmark treating the model as the independent variable. Beyond merely flying toward a pixel, our agent entrusts the model to yaw and search, deliberate when unsure, and self-declare arrival---all without fine-tuning or function-calling schemas. Evaluating frontier and open models across four core capabilities---approaching a visible target, tracking a moving one, searching outside the initial view, and commanding a multi-drone fleet---reveals that even the simplest embodied settings are far from solved. Crucially, to identify what breaks first at the edge, our roster scales down to 2B parameters. The findings expose a stark paradox: it is not the flying that fails. Small open models often navigate into the success radius more reliably than frontier models, yet lose the episode by declaring arrival prematurely or not at all. Multi-drone commanding amplifies this divide, with small models failing by blindly copying a single coordinate across distinct views. Viewed as vision-language-action agents, the models' spatial perception holds up, but their action protocol does not. What separates a deployable edge model from a frontier model is not navigation, but the discipline to sustain a declared protocol and emit the correct terminating action. The open problem is closing this gap at onboard compute costs---yielding a fast model that plans persistently and knows exactly when it is done---and DroneCATS is built to measure that distance.

title: Value Over Language Model: Detecting Original Contribution in Writing
abstract: LLMs have been rapidly adopted across writing tasks, prompting the development of tools for detecting LLM-generated text. Yet, these tools largely measure how much of a document's surface text was written by an LLM and aren't fundamentally designed to measure how much of the information content or ideas originated from the LLM itself rather than being supplied by the user in the prompt. In this work, we design a framework that measures how much value a person adds on top of what a language model could have easily produced by itself. The method requires no training or labeled data and never scores the document's surface text, insulating it from stylistic confounders. Instead, it extracts the document's content at increasing levels of granularity, uses an LLM to reconstruct the document from each partial representation, and compares these reconstructions with those produced from the task description alone. We call this framework Value Over Language Model (VOLM), which measures a document's contribution relative to a replacement-level document that an LLM could produce from the task description alone. We evaluate VOLM with a specific instantiation of this framework across three domains: news articles, ICLR peer reviews, and argumentative essays. VOLM separates human-authored documents from matched LLM-generated documents produced from generic task descriptions, while remaining substantially invariant to content-preserving transformations, including LLM-based reconstruction and round-trip translation. We further find that increasingly constrained content extractors reduce residual differences between LLM-generated and humanized text, demonstrating the importance of disentangling informational content from stylistic variation. We hope these results encourage further work on specialized instantiations of the framework and on assessing human contributions in LLM-assisted writing more generally.

title: Semi-Supervised Classification with Informative Missing Labels in Weibull Mixture Models
abstract: We consider semi-supervised classification from a partially classified sample arising from a two-component Weibull mixture. The feature is observed for all data, whereas some class labels are missing. The probability of a missing label is modelled as a function of classification uncertainty, giving a feature-dependent missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism that shares parameters with the Weibull-mixture classifier. The missing-label indicators can therefore provide information about the classifier in addition to the observed features and available class labels. Under a common Weibull shape, a Bayes' rule has at most one positive decision boundary, which is unique when the rule is nonconstant; under unequal shapes, it can have two. We characterise these decision regions, derive the Fisher information for the classifier after adjustment for nuisance parameters in the missingness model, and obtain a decision-boundary expansion of the expected error rate of the plug-in sample rule relative to the Bayes error. The expansion yields classification-specific asymptotic relative efficiency formulas for the one- and two-boundary cases and shows that a positive-definite increase in Fisher information is sufficient, but not necessary, for a smaller first-order expected error rate. Numerical studies and a semi-synthetic analysis based on hard-drive failure data illustrate potential reductions in expected error rate and improvements in decision-boundary estimation from modelling feature-dependent label missingness.

title: Ranked by the Matcher: A Reproducibility Audit of Knowledge Graph Extraction from Threat Reports
abstract: Security teams and researchers choose knowledge-graph extraction tooling for threat reports on the strength of published triple-F1 scores, yet those scores depend on how predicted triples are matched to gold annotations. We could reimplement the stated matching rule for only five of twelve inspected systems. Re-scoring ten system outputs on shared documents under eight protocols reverses eleven of forty-five pairwise orderings; one fixed prediction set spans 0.16--0.70 F1. On an external, human-adjudicated set, no mechanical matcher---lexical, embedding, or entailment---agrees with the reviewers more than seven times in ten; an LLM judge agrees far more often. To separate component effects from matcher rewards, we build CTIForge, whose deterministic validation layer can vary while extraction is held byte-identical. Across seven tested deployment configurations, no hosted backbone loses precision under validation and every offline one does. Backbone, decoding, and prompting covary across those configurations; on the one backbone we could serve both ways, serving alone reproduces the split. It coincides with a roughly 2.8-fold increase in actions explicitly disputing entity type, consistent with hand-written rules encoding the conventions of the extractor against which they were developed. We release the pipeline, protocol suite, and per-triple audit records.

evidence.title: Ranked by the Matcher: A Reproducibility Audit of Knowledge Graph Extraction from Threat Reports
evidence.abstract: Security teams and researchers choose knowledge-graph extraction tooling for threat reports on the strength of published triple-F1 scores, yet those scores depend on how predicted triples are matched to gold annotations. We could reimplement the stated matching rule for only five of twelve inspected systems. Re-scoring ten system outputs on shared documents under eight protocols reverses eleven of forty-five pairwise orderings; one fixed prediction set spans 0.16--0.70 F1. On an external, human-adjudicated set, no mechanical matcher---lexical, embedding, or entailment---agrees with the reviewers more than seven times in ten; an LLM judge agrees far more often. To separate component effects from matcher rewards, we build CTIForge, whose deterministic validation layer can vary while extraction is held byte-identical. Across seven tested deployment configurations, no hosted backbone loses precision under validation and every offline one does. Backbone, decoding, and prompting covary across those configurations; on the one backbone we could serve both ways, serving alone reproduces the split. It coincides with a roughly 2.8-fold increase in actions explicitly disputing entity type, consistent with hand-written rules encoding the conventions of the extractor against which they were developed. We release the pipeline, protocol suite, and per-triple audit records.

title: Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning
abstract: A major question in cognitive modeling concerns the behavioral alignment between large language models and humans across linguistic and non-linguistic tasks. Unlike standard LLMs, large reasoning models (LRMs) are optimized with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, encouraging correct solutions to reasoning tasks rather than preference-aligned responses. Recent work (de Varda et al., 2025) investigates the cost of thinking in humans and LRMs by comparing human reaction times with model reasoning traces across a range of reasoning tasks. We isolate this alignment by turning to abductive reasoning: unlike deductive tasks, its difficulty cannot be inferred from formal structure and offers no shortcuts a model could exploit to mimic effort without genuine search, providing firmer ground for empirical claims of shared effort. We find further evidence of alignment between LRM and human reasoning effort, as well as evidence that models and humans tend to make similar errors. Finally, we show that decoding methods that let models explore multiple reasoning paths increase alignment in reasoning cost between humans and LRMs across the three models tested.

title: VakyArth: Evaluating Pragmatic Competence in LLMs across Indic Languages
abstract: Real-world communication often requires pragmatic reasoning: interpreting meanings implied through context and cultural convention rather than stated literally. Existing pragmatic evaluation remains largely limited to English and high-resource languages, leaving Indic languages unexplored despite their linguistic and cultural diversity. We introduce VakyArth, the first pragmatic benchmark for Indic languages, designed as a diagnostic evaluation covering Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Malayalam. VakyArth evaluates models across five phenomena: deixis, speech acts, implicature, social pragmatics, and coherence; through multiple-choice questions, natural language inference, and translation, with all items authored by native speakers. Across multilingual large language models (LLMs) of varying families and sizes, we find consistent failures on pragmatic meanings rooted in Indic linguistic and cultural conventions. Our analysis shows systematic differences across languages and tasks: MCQ accuracy exceeds NLI accuracy in all model-language combinations, translation performance does not reliably track pragmatic understanding, and Indo-Aryan languages show a translation advantage over Dravidian languages. We further show that automatic translation metrics can miss fluent but pragmatically unfaithful outputs, especially for implicature and deixis.

title: KriseSens: : Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Disaster Monitoring and Classification System Using LSTM and Cloud Deployment
abstract: Natural disasters like earthquakes, floods, cyclones, and wildfires are happening more often and with more force. Thismakes it very important to keep an eye on disaster in real time a problem for everyone. Current platforms havefragmented, unstructured data that isn't processed intelligently, which makes them less useful in situations where timeis of the essence. This paper introduces KriseSens – Disaster Monitor, a web-based Crisis Alert and Monitoring Systemthat consolidates automated data aggregation, Natural Language Processing-driven preprocessing, deep learningclassification, and interactive visualization into a cohesive platform. RSS parsing is used to collect real-time disaster feedsfrom the Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (GDACS) and the United States Geological Survey (USGS). ATensorFlow-based LSTM deep learning model, trained on the CrisisLexT6 benchmark dataset, sorts incoming text datainto disaster types (earthquake, flood, cyclone, wildfire) with a certain level of confidence of 0.95. The Python Flaskbackend runs on Hugging Face Spaces and has RESTful API endpoints (/live-feed,/classify) that a responsive HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend hosted on Vercel can use. The interactive glassmorphismstyledashboard shows alerts that are grouped by type on a global crisis map. It also lets you filter alerts by type and hasa manual text classifier. Functional testing showed that all five test modules—data collection, preprocessing,classification, API, and frontend—worked. The system shows that AI-driven disaster monitoring can work and providesa scalable base for future improvements like predictive analytics, real-time push notifications, GIS integration, andtransformer-based NLP models.

title: Constructing handwritten grammatical error correction dataset for CSL learners: methodology and application
abstract: Current research on Chinese grammatical error correction mainly relies on printed text datasets and lacks dedicated data for handwritten text. Accordingly, a handwriting Chinese grammatical error correction dataset for Chinese as a second language learners was constructed. Using authentic handwritten compositions as the corpus, an optimized optical character recognition system was employed to process noise such as overwriting and revisions. Through text recognition, standardized annotation, image-text alignment, and quality validation, fine-grained, multi-modal annotated data was generated. The dataset comprises 8 726 valid samples, covering 599 fine-grained error types, and can provide data support for grammatical error correction, error diagnosis, and intelligent Chinese language teaching in handwriting scenarios.

title: Polar Clustering and Stabilized Cluster Likelihoods for Extended Object Maritime Radar Tracking
abstract: Accurate maritime situational awareness is essential for safety, security, and environmental protection. While the Automatic Identification System (AIS) is widely used, it is vulnerable to jamming, spoofing, and intentional manipulation. These limitations can be mitigated through independent validation using marine X-band radars, where high-resolution coastal sensors detect extended targets with distance-dependent sparsity and raw data in polar coordinates. This paper evaluates a polar-domain clustering algorithm together with its impact on a family of extended-object multi-target tracking (MTT) frameworks of increasing complexity. A Random Matrix Model (RMM) based estimator incorporating radar intensity information is useed for a combined centroid and extension tracking. Beyond the front end, we detail the tracker mathematics required for robust operation on high-resolution clusters. The modifications include a stabilized cluster-likelihood formulation that avoids the clutter-power penalty of point-based extended-object models, a fully log-domain hypothesis-generation backbone shared by the IPDA, JIPDA, and PHD filters, and a measurement-driven birth (MDB) model that removes the one-frame latency of the classical Gaussian-mixture PHD. Performance is validated on real-world X-band radar data within selected Regions of Interest (ROI) and at different distances from the sensor. Results show that clustering in the polar domain is more robust against the distance variability of detections and benefits the overall performance of the tracking algorithms.

title: A Key-Switching Protocol for the Homomorphic Encryption of IoT Data
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a growing field, and, as such, we must prioritise the security of data held within these devices due to their vulnerability, as they are commonly low-powered or unprotected.There exist homomorphic encryption schemes that allow secure computations on data from IoT devices.Still, they come at the cost of latency, and those with low latency come at the cost of security.The protocol presented in this paper suggests a way to reduce overhead latency timings whilst maintaining security during data transmission.This is done through key-switching, allowing the data owner to choose parties who are allowed to act on the plaintext rather than the ciphertext.Additionally, if a party is not trusted, the client and server can continue computing on homomorphically encrypted data, allowing for an uninterrupted workflow.The outlined protocol is created using the OpenFHE Library in C++ and tested on Google Cloud against the protocol in [1].The protocol improves system performance, with an average 53.86% reduction in average latency and an average 5.98 percentage point reduction in average CPU utilisation.

title: Identifikasi Kebutuhan Infrastruktur Transportasi Berbasis Analisis Sentimen Media Sosial di Kabupaten Lamongan
abstract: Perencanaan infrastruktur transportasi membutuhkan data teknis sekaligus persepsi masyarakat sebagai pengguna. Media sosial kini menjadi sumber data alternatif yang kaya akan opini dan keluhan publik. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengidentifikasi kebutuhan serta menentukan tingkat dan lokasi prioritas penanganan infrastruktur transportasi di Kabupaten Lamongan berdasarkan sentimen masyarakat di media sosial. Penelitian kuantitatif ini menggunakan metode text mining, machine learning, topic modeling, dan analisis spasial berbasis GIS. Data media sosial dikumpulkan berdasarkan kata kunci terkait transportasi lalu melalui tahapan preprocessing (cleansing, case folding, tokenizing, normalization, stopword removal, dan stemming). Analisis sentimen dilakukan menggunakan pembobotan TF-IDF dan algoritma Support Vector Machine (SVM). Identifikasi isu utama memanfaatkan Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), yang kemudian dikombinasikan dengan data teknis melalui skoring berbobot dan divisualisasikan dengan GIS. Hasil analisis dari 1.500 sampel data menunjukkan distribusi sentimen negatif sebesar 58%, netral 27%, dan positif 15%. Lima topik permasalahan utama yang teridentifikasi meliputi kerusakan jalan, kemacetan, keselamatan transportasi, penerangan serta rambu/marka, dan fasilitas pejalan kaki. Model klasifikasi SVM menghasilkan akurasi 87%, precision 86%, recall 85%, dan F1-score 85,5%. Temuan ini membuktikan bahwa pengolahan data media sosial yang dipadukan dengan pemetaan GIS mampu memberikan indikasi awal serta memetakan prioritas penanganan masalah transportasi secara efektif. Dengan demikian, pendekatan ini dapat menjadi instrumen pendukung perencanaan infrastruktur di Kabupaten Lamongan, meski tetap memerlukan verifikasi lapangan sebelum keputusan akhir diambil.

title: Runtime Pass Is Not Correctness: A Negative Reasoning-Efficiency Post-Training Result and Verifier Audit on Qwen3.8-27B
abstract: P-BREVE-01-R2 reports a negative reasoning-efficiency post-training result and an evaluator-audit result on Qwen3.8-27B. No model, bank, or release candidate resulted. Scope: a development-tier result on one model lineage; the replacement verifier bank is not qualified; the superseded adequacy claim is withdrawn; reported rates characterise the audited evaluation set and do not estimate ordinary product traffic. No model checkpoint is recommended, released, or promoted on the basis of this report.

title: CV2F★: Combining CryptoVerif and F★ for Proving Security of Protocol Implementations
abstract: This artifact provides the CV2F* development and the Sesame case study described in the paper "CV2F*: Combining CryptoVerif and F* for Proving Security of Protocol Implementations", to be presented at the ACM Conference on Computer Security (CCS), 2026. The artifact contains a distribution of the CryptoVerif protocol verifier, on top of which we built the CV2F* framework. We provide the artifact packaged as a ready-to-use Docker image (cv2fstar.tar.gz), as well as the sources (cryptoverif-sources.tar.gz) and Dockerfile allowing to rebuild a Docker image from scratch.

title: Cape York Melomys-Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, the Cape York Melomys-Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm (CYMMA), designed for tackling complex optimization problems. The algorithm's core inspiration stems from the foraging behavior of *Melomys rubicola*, a unique rodent species endemic to the Cape York Peninsula in Australia, known for its efficient and adaptive foraging strategies. CYMMA incorporates elements of the melomys's spatial memory, exploratory behavior, and social interaction into its design. Specifically, the algorithm utilizes a modified particle representation based on the melomys's memory map, a dynamic exploration strategy mimicking its movement patterns, and a collaborative learning mechanism inspired by the social dynamics observed in melomys colonies. The algorithm is formally described using mathematical notation. The performance of CYMMA is evaluated through simulations on a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency compared to established metaheuristic algorithms. Key performance metrics, including convergence rate, solution quality, and computational cost, are analyzed. The results indicate that CYMMA is a promising approach for solving challenging optimization problems across diverse domains. The algorithm's design principles and potential applications are discussed, highlighting its adaptability and potential for further development.

title: Adaptive Circuit Synthesis Based on Evolutionary Algorithms and Circuit Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to digital circuit synthesis leveraging the power of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) combined with real-time circuit simulation. The core idea is to utilize an EA to generate a population of circuit designs, followed by iterative evaluation and feedback from a circuit simulator. This closed-loop system allows for adaptive optimization, ensuring that the synthesized circuits continuously meet specified performance criteria. The key contribution lies in the integration of these two powerful techniques, creating a dynamic design process where the EA adjusts its search strategy based on simulation results. This approach demonstrates the potential for efficient and automated circuit design, particularly for complex designs where traditional methods may struggle to find optimal solutions. The paper outlines the methodology, including the EA's genetic operators, the simulation environment, and the feedback mechanism. Finally, it discusses the potential benefits and challenges of this adaptive synthesis technique.

title: Bushman Hare: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Bushman Hare Behavior
abstract: This paper presents Bushman Hare, a new metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of Bushman hares. The algorithm leverages the hare's strategic movement patterns—particularly its tendency to explore diverse areas and return to previously successful locations—to guide the search process. Bushman Hare incorporates a novel adaptive exploration-exploitation strategy, utilizing a 'hare's memory' to prioritize areas with recent successful solutions. The algorithm employs a population-based approach with a dynamically adjusted carrying capacity and a novel 'hare trail' mechanism to enhance exploration. Performance evaluations using a suite of benchmark functions demonstrate that Bushman Hare achieves competitive results compared to established metaheuristic algorithms like Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The core of the algorithm is defined by the following key equations: * Population Update: $V_{ij}(t+1) = \eta_1 \cdot V_{ij}(t) + \eta_2 \cdot R_{ij} \cdot (X_{best,j} - X_{ij}(t))$ * Carrying Capacity Adjustment: $C(t+1) = C(t) + \alpha \cdot (N - |S(t)|)$ * Hare Trail Update: $Trail(t+1) = Trail(t) + \beta \cdot (S(t) - S(t-1))$ Where: $V_{ij}(t)$ is the velocity of particle *i* in dimension *j* at generation *t*. $R_{ij}$ is a random number between 0 and 1. $X_{best,j}$ is the best value of dimension *j* across the entire population. $C(t)$ is the carrying capacity at generation *t*. $N$ is the population size. $S(t)$ is the set of successful solutions at generation *t*. $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are parameters controlling the carrying capacity and trail update rates, respectively. The algorithm's effectiveness is primarily attributed to the balance between maintaining a diverse population through the carrying capacity adjustment and focusing on promising regions through the hare trail mechanism.

title: Adaptive High-Dimensional Machine Learning with Dynamic Spatial Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive high-dimensional machine learning framework that integrates a machine learning model with a dynamic spatial modeling approach. The framework dynamically adjusts spatial parameters to optimize model parameters, enhancing performance in complex geometric scenarios. We propose a novel method for parameter optimization based on a spatial modeling framework, providing a significant advancement over static parameterization techniques. The core mechanism involves coupling the model with a spatial representation, dynamically adjusting spatial parameters to improve model adaptability and generalization. This research addresses a critical challenge in high-dimensional machine learning, specifically in situations where geometric complexities significantly impact model performance. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in improving model robustness and accuracy across diverse geometric datasets.

title: ##基于量子信息论的软件加密算法
abstract: This paper proposes a novel software encryption algorithm based on the principles of quantum information theory. The core claim is to develop an encryption scheme offering enhanced security compared to traditional cryptographic methods. The proposed algorithm leverages quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols and the inherent properties of quantum states, specifically superposition and entanglement, to construct a highly secure encryption system. Traditional cryptographic algorithms are vulnerable to attacks from quantum computers, while algorithms rooted in quantum information theory provide a significantly higher level of security. This research details the theoretical framework, key components, and security analysis of the algorithm, highlighting its potential to address the growing threat posed by quantum computing to existing encryption standards. The algorithm's design emphasizes resilience against known classical and quantum attacks. The system relies on the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics to ensure a high degree of uncertainty and complexity, making it significantly more difficult to break. This work presents a foundational approach for developing quantum-resistant cryptographic solutions. ---

title: ## Broad-toothed Mouse Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper introduces a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the Broad-toothed Mouse Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm (BMMIA), motivated by the foraging behavior of *Mus minutulus* (broad-toothed mouse). The algorithm leverages the mouse's ability to efficiently navigate complex environments and identify promising regions for food sources. BMMIA incorporates a unique exploration strategy based on simulated whisker movements and a novel convergence mechanism inspired by the mouse's adaptation to changing food availability. The algorithm's core components include a position representation, a fitness evaluation function, and an adaptive parameter control mechanism. We demonstrate the efficacy of BMMIA through application to several benchmark optimization problems, showcasing its competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic methods such as the Genetic Algorithm (GA) and the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The results highlight the algorithm's potential for solving complex optimization challenges where efficient exploration and exploitation are critical. Finally, we discuss the algorithm's limitations and suggest future research directions.

title: Broad-headed Tree Mouse Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the "Broad-headed Tree Mouse Algorithm" (BHTMA), inspired by the foraging behavior of the broad-headed tree mouse ( *Tragma coenurus*). This algorithm leverages the mouse's ability to efficiently navigate complex, three-dimensional environments to find optimal solutions in challenging optimization problems. The BHTMA incorporates key features of the mouse's behavior, including path exploration, obstacle avoidance, and the utilization of hierarchical structures, into a search strategy. The algorithm utilizes a population-based approach with a novel movement mechanism simulating the tree mouse's exploration. The performance of the BHTMA is evaluated through a series of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency compared to established metaheuristic algorithms such as the Genetic Algorithm (GA) and the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The results show that the BHTMA is capable of finding near-optimal solutions within reasonable computational time for a range of problems, indicating its potential for practical applications in diverse fields. The core of the algorithm involves a dynamic tree representation, a novel movement probability function, and an adaptive mutation operator, all contributing to its robustness and adaptability.

title: Title: Quantum Machine Learning for Non-Standard Data Sets
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) offers a paradigm shift in data analysis, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical machine learning algorithms with its capacity for enhanced pattern recognition and data representation. This paper explores the application of quantum algorithms to address the challenges posed by inherently non-standard datasets, such as sensor data and time-series data characterized by complex correlations and high dimensionality. We propose a novel framework centered on quantum principal component analysis (QPCA) and Grover's algorithm to extract key insights from these datasets, demonstrating potential improvements in data understanding and feature extraction. This work aims to establish a foundation for QML applications in diverse fields, including anomaly detection, predictive modeling, and signal processing, where traditional methods often fall short. The core mechanism involves leveraging quantum properties to overcome challenges inherent in these data types.

title: Title: Algorithmic Complexity Reduction through Quantum Parallelism
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum parallelism to dramatically reduce the computational complexity of a specific problem. We introduce a novel quantum algorithm designed to exploit quantum circuits and distributed parallelism to achieve significant performance gains compared to classical approaches. The core mechanism centers on the execution of independent quantum circuits on multiple qubits, effectively increasing the overall number of operations performed. This research investigates the feasibility of this approach and presents a preliminary design with a focus on demonstrating a substantial reduction in computational steps. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and the potential impact of this technology.

title: Probability Logic Circuits
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of probability logic circuits, a novel approach to computation that leverages probabilistic logic gates to handle uncertainty and ambiguity. Traditional logic circuits operate on deterministic data, limiting their applicability in domains dealing with inherent randomness or incomplete information. Probability logic circuits, built upon gates such as probabilistic AND, probabilistic OR, and probabilistic NOT, offer a mechanism for simulating logical behavior through probabilistic operations. This approach provides a framework for representing and processing uncertain information, potentially leading to advancements in areas like artificial intelligence and robotics. The core claim is that these circuits provide a more flexible computing paradigm. This document details the foundational concepts and mechanics of this new circuit design, outlining its potential advantages and future research directions.

title: Blind Mole: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Behavior of a Blind Mole
abstract: This paper presents Blind Mole, a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of blind moles. The algorithm leverages the mole's ability to navigate and find food in a dark environment by utilizing a combination of local search, probabilistic exploration, and a "memory" mechanism to retain promising regions of the search space. Blind Mole employs a particle representation where each particle embodies a potential solution. The algorithm operates within a defined search space, iteratively refining solutions through a series of steps including position updates, velocity updates, and a "pheromone" mechanism. The core innovation lies in the mole's "blind" characteristic, which is simulated by a stochastic exploration strategy that biases the algorithm towards unexplored areas, preventing premature convergence to local optima. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions within reasonable computational time. The key features of Blind Mole include its adaptability, robust exploration, and efficient convergence properties, making it a viable alternative to established metaheuristic methods. The algorithm's design promotes both exploration and exploitation, resulting in a balance between discovering new solutions and refining existing ones. The experimental results show promising performance across various problem types.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction with Geometric Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm for solving constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) – a fundamental problem in computer science and artificial intelligence – by integrating quantum annealing and geometric modeling. We propose a framework where the problem space is represented as a geometric object, and quantum annealing is used to efficiently explore this object and identify promising solutions. The core mechanism hinges on exploiting geometric properties to guide the quantum annealing process, leading to improved speed and solution quality compared to classical approaches. The integration of geometric modeling offers a unique pathway to enhance the problem-solving capabilities of quantum computers, potentially unlocking new possibilities in constraint satisfaction. This work explores the potential of this approach and presents preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness.

title: Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) Simulation and Optimization Techniques
abstract: Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) represents a crucial component in the realization of practical quantum computers, enabling fast and probabilistic data access for quantum algorithms. However, accurately simulating QRAM's operation presents a formidable challenge due to the inherent randomness and quantum mechanical nature of the system. This work investigates and proposes novel simulation techniques and optimization algorithms aimed at mitigating this computational complexity. We explore various approaches, including stochastic simulation methods, reduced-order modeling, and tailored optimization strategies, focusing on minimizing the number of quantum operations required for accurate QRAM simulation. The results demonstrate significant reductions in computational cost while maintaining a reasonable level of fidelity, paving the way for more efficient design and analysis of QRAM architectures. The core claim of this research is that the development of QRAM is fundamentally limited by the complexity of its simulation, and this work offers a direct path toward overcoming this bottleneck.

title: Investigating the Relationship between Objective AI-driven Metrics and Subjective MOS for In-the-Wild Speech
abstract: Automated Mean Opinion Score (MOS) predictors are widely used for TTS evaluation but are trained on studio or denoising corpora. Compared to human MOS ratings, O-MOS correlations collapse on in-the-wild (ITW) discrete-token TTS. We conduct a controlled ablation across four systems—continuous clean TTS, discrete ITW TTS (MQTTS), an additive noise control, and ground-truth recordings—and collect 768 human naturalness ratings under a headphone-screened protocol. UTMOSv2 correlation collapses from r=0.51 (p<0.01) on the continuous clean system to r=−0.01 (n.s.) on the discrete ITW system; other neural predictors also collapse. DNSMOS P.835 penalises an additive noise condition 0.42 points more severely than a generative-artefact condition despite listeners rating both equivalently, directly contradicting human perception. These findings challenge the validity of current objective metrics as standalone proxies for naturalness evaluation of inthe-wild generative TTS.
